title: A Deeper Understanding of Javascript Objects
summary: Explains JavaScript objects as bundles of related properties, why they beat many separate variables, and how constructor functions with the new keyword mass-produce objects with the same shape. Uses a hotel staff scenario (bellboys, housekeepers) with two build-it-yourself challenges.

concepts.heading: The problem with separate variables
points: Storing each fact about a person in its own variable (e.g. bellBoy1Name, bellBoy1Age...) works for one person but doesn't scale: each new person needs a new set of variables with invented names.
The mental model is a table or spreadsheet: one row per property, one column per individual, with the same properties for each.

concepts.heading: Object literals
points: Create one with var name = { ... }. Curly braces enclose comma-separated property: value pairs.
Property names follow variable naming conventions: camelCase, not starting with a digit.
Values can be any type: string, number, boolean, array, even a function.
Read a value with dot notation: bellBoy1.name. In an alert this becomes a greeting built by string concatenation.
Different kinds of thing get different properties: a housekeeper might record yearsOfExperience, name and a cleaningRepertoire array.
Structured data like this is less error-prone than loose variables.

concepts.heading: Constructor functions
points: Writing out every property for every new object is repetitive. A constructor function is a template (the lecture compares it to a factory) that builds objects for you.
Convention: the function name starts with a capital letter (BellBoy, Housekeeper), which signals it is a constructor and not an ordinary function.
Its parameters are the values supplied per object. Inside, assign each to a property of the object being built: this.name = name; this.yearsOfExperience = yearsOfExperience; and so on.
Create objects by calling it with the new keyword: var houseKeeper1 = new Housekeeper(9, "Tom", ["Lobby", "Bedroom"]). Arguments must follow the parameter order.
The only syntactic difference from calling a normal function is new plus the capitalised name. Omitting new breaks the pattern (this would not refer to a fresh object).
After creating, access properties via the dot: houseKeeper1.name gives "Tom".
Many objects with identical properties but different values can then be created in one line each.

concepts.heading: Workflow notes
points: The Chrome DevTools Sources tab (snippets) is used to run the code; a hard reload clears earlier definitions.

task.name: Housekeeper object and constructor
task.goal: First build a single object literal, then replace it with a constructor function and create objects from it.
steps: Declare var houseKeeper1 = { ... } with properties of your choice (e.g. yearsOfExperience, name, cleaningRepertoire array).
Write a capitalised constructor Housekeeper(...) taking one parameter per property and assigning each to this.
Delete the literal and create objects with new Housekeeper(...) giving values in parameter order.
Log a property from the new object to confirm.
task.expected_result: Logging the name of an object built via new prints the value you passed in; additional objects take one line each.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 18 - Advanced Javascript and DOM Manipulation/18.05 - A Deeper Understanding of Javascript Objects/script.js

pitfalls: Forgetting new when calling a constructor.
Passing constructor arguments in a different order from the parameters.
Starting a constructor name with a lowercase letter (works, but breaks the convention).
Missing commas between properties in an object literal (no comma after the last one is needed).
(Extra) The lecture's housekeeper constructor has parameters in the order experience, name, repertoire; the reference repo uses name first. Either is fine if calls match.
(Extra) Defining a method inside the constructor (this.clean = function...) creates a separate copy per object; prototypes avoid this but are beyond this lesson.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet (section 18 has no playground file).
gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'Objects and constructors': tasks: (1) turn five loose variables into an object, (2) read and update properties with dot notation, (3) write a constructor, (4) create three instances, (5) add a method.
Interactive demo: a form that fills constructor arguments and renders the resulting object as a table, with a live console showing property reads.
